r: The course surveys recreation and leisure philosophy, history, career pathways, and the interrelationships among governmental, voluntary, institutional, and commercial recreation agencies — an entirely expository body of knowledge delivered through lecture and reading rather than fieldwork. This maps to Getting Information and Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge, activities task-exposure research classifies among the more automatable knowledge-transmission categories, since AI already drafts competent sector overviews and career-path explanations. The course carries no general-studies transfer designation and no clinical or licensure lock, so little institutional weight protects it, though as the entry point for the therapeutic-recreation sequence it retains a modest foundational role capping erosion at this horizon only. Observed-usage data shows informational and explanatory tasks growing as a share of AI use, but classroom diffusion remains limited at 24 months, so the instrumental need to enroll is only partially eroded. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently deliver survey-level content on recreation philosophy, history, and agency structure, and plausibly tutor students directly through career-pathway guidance, eroding the rationale for a lecture-based overview course. The foundational cap that holds the course to Medium at 24 months applies only at that horizon per the rubric, so it no longer bounds the rating here. No general-studies mandate, licensure requirement, or embodiment protects the course's informational content; the applied work — explaining agency relationships and career options — sits squarely in the highly-exposed, low-verification-burden knowledge-transmission category the task-exposure literature associates with writers and explainers. Diffusion of capable AI tutoring into gateway courses is plausible by this horizon even if not yet realized system-wide. The rating rises to High: the instrumental case for a human-taught survey of this specific content is substantially eroded, though genuine uncertainty remains about how introductory courses restructure pedagogically.

A decade out, AI explanation and tutoring of introductory recreation-field content is a mature capability, and the central case has such material delivered adaptively and personally rather than through a required standalone course. Nothing in the course's structure — no clinical hours, no general-studies lock, no deep foundational dependency beyond the entry-level prerequisite already accounted for — resists that trajectory, and the capability-trend evidence on compute and task-horizon growth supports continued gains through 2036. The rating holds High, hedged by the wide uncertainty inherent to any ten-year forecast and by the possibility that institutions restructure gateway courses around AI tools rather than eliminating them outright. What is comparatively clear is that the specific instrumental rationale — a human lecturing students through agency history and career philosophy — is the kind of task this evidence base consistently places among the most exposed, absent a binding institutional or embodied constraint.
RECR 1870.d: This course provides an overview of recreation and leisure, including career opportunities. Philosophy, history, leisure education, and the interrelationships among governmental institutional, voluntary, and commercial/private recreation and park agencies are discussed.

r: This course develops and enhances recreation leadership skills used in the delivery of recreation and park services — leading games, group activities, and program sessions in real time with participants. The applied work maps to Performing for or Working Directly with the Public and Guiding, Directing, and Motivating Subordinates, activities task-exposure research consistently places among the least automatable because they require live, embodied, in-person facilitation and split-second interpersonal adjustment. Verification of leadership competence also depends on watching a person actually lead a group, not on evaluating written output. There is no general-studies designation and no licensure lock, but embodiment alone does the protective work here. At 24 months there is no meaningful erosion: an AI system can describe leadership techniques, but it cannot lead a recreation group, and the course's instrumental purpose is the student's own embodied leadership capacity.

By 2031, AI planning tools may help students draft session outlines or game plans, offloading some preparatory work, and diffusion data suggests such assistive tools will be more common in program offices by this horizon. But the graded, applied competence this course builds — standing in front of a group and leading it competently and safely through activity — remains a live, real-time, psychomotor and interpersonal skill that automation does not perform on the student's behalf. Verification burden stays low-protective because assessing leadership requires direct observation of the person leading, not review of a document. No institutional mandate binds the course, but embodiment alone holds the rating at Low across a full catalog cycle; diffusion of capable AI into embodied group-facilitation delivery itself is not a plausible near-term development regardless of how much planning support improves.

Even under a central case of substantial capability growth by 2036, driven by the fast pace of underlying model and compute trends, the specific competence Recreation Leadership Skills and Techniques builds — leading people through activity in person, reading a group's energy, and adjusting in real time — sits within the task-exposure literature's least-automatable category of live interpersonal and physical performance. AI may become a more capable planning assistant for session design, but that does not substitute for the embodied leadership act itself. The rating holds Low with reasonable confidence; the honest uncertainty concerns how much preparatory and administrative work around leadership shifts to AI tools, not whether the applied leadership competence remains instrumentally necessary for a student pursuing recreation delivery roles.
RECR 2110.d: This course is designed to develop and enhance recreation leadership skills used in the delivery of recreation and park services.

r: The course surveys the recreation needs of individuals with disabilities and provides an overview of therapeutic recreation service delivery across health-care and community-based settings — informational and conceptual content taught through lecture and reading rather than direct client contact. This maps to Getting Information and Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge, categories AI already handles competently when explaining service models and population needs. The course carries no general-studies lock, but it is the hard prerequisite substrate for every subsequent therapeutic-recreation course in the sequence — programming, techniques, issues and trends, advanced techniques — making it critical foundational scaffolding that caps the rating regardless of how exposed the survey content itself becomes. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this base knowledge before advancing is intact; AI can explain TR service models, but the course exists to ground the entire specialization built on top of it.

By 2031, AI will fluently explain disability-related recreation needs and TR service structures, eroding the rationale for a human-delivered survey of this factual content. But because the course is foundational scaffolding for the entire therapeutic-recreation sequence, the rubric's foundational cap holds the rating at Medium regardless of how automatable the underlying overview content becomes — every later required TR course depends on the conceptual base this course establishes. The instrumental case shifts from information delivery toward the grounding a student needs before working with clinical assessment, programming, and technique courses that assume this literacy. Task-exposure research classifies informational survey content as increasingly AI-deliverable, which pushes exposure upward, while the prerequisite structure holds the course in the curriculum across a catalog cycle. Rating Medium.

A decade out, AI is a fluent and authoritative explainer of disability-related recreation needs and therapeutic-recreation service models, and the pure information-transmission rationale for the course is substantially eroded. But the foundational-scaffolding cap persists in the central case: the entire upper-division TR sequence — programming, assessment techniques, advanced facilitation, professional issues — is built on the conceptual base this course establishes, and that structural dependency does not loosen merely because AI can explain the content well. The rating holds Medium, capped from High by foundational role rather than by any licensure or embodiment factor. The genuine uncertainty is pedagogical — how the survey content is taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI explanation — not whether the grounding role for downstream coursework remains instrumentally necessary.
RECR 3330.d: This course surveys the recreation needs of individuals with disabilities. It provides an overview to therapeutic recreation services, including those in both health-care agencies and community-based settings.

r: The course teaches program-development concepts — conceptualization, planning, implementation, and evaluation of comprehensive and specific therapeutic recreation services, along with equipment and program modifications and adaptations. This is administrative and analytical program-management work, mapping to Developing Objectives and Strategies and Scheduling Work and Activities, categories where AI already drafts program plans, evaluation frameworks, and adaptation documentation competently. Unlike the survey and technique courses in the sequence, this course is not itself a prerequisite for other required TR coursework, so no foundational scaffolding caps its exposure, and it carries no general-studies designation or accreditation credit-hour floor. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI meaningfully assists program-planning documents, partially eroding the instrumental case, but near-term classroom diffusion into how programming is actually taught keeps the realized effect only partial.

By 2031, AI will competently generate program plans, evaluation frameworks, and adaptation strategies for therapeutic recreation services — the applied planning and documentation tasks this course's knowledge serves — and observed-usage data shows business-and-planning tasks as a growing share of AI use. With no general-studies lock, no licensure-gated clinical hours specific to this course, and no downstream foundational dependency, little institutionally protects the rating from rising. The residual competence — judging whether a proposed adaptation actually serves a client population well — is real but narrower than the full conceptualize-plan-implement-evaluate content this course teaches. The rating is High: the applied program-development work is performed competently by AI with limited human input for most of the planning artifacts involved, even as some site-specific adaptation judgment remains with the practitioner.

A decade out, AI is deeply capable at generating and refining recreation program plans, evaluation designs, and equipment-adaptation documentation, and the applied planning work to which this course's knowledge is put is largely automatable. With no institutional lock and no foundational role protecting it, the instrumental case for a course centered on teaching students to conceptualize and document programs manually is substantially eroded. The rating is High, hedged by the possibility that judgment about adapting programs for specific client needs retains a verification premium AI planning tools do not fully replace, and by the general uncertainty of a ten-year horizon. Among the therapeutic-recreation courses in this batch, this program-management content is the most exposed precisely because nothing embodied or institutionally binding holds it back.
RECR 3430.d: This course focuses on applying programming concepts including conceptualization, planning, implementation, and evaluation of comprehensive and specific therapeutic recreation services. Equipment, program modifications, and adaptations are discussed.

r: The course examines tools, techniques, and procedures used in delivering therapeutic recreation services — assessment, individual treatment and program plans, documentation, and community integration skills — and explicitly requires application of this content to practice in the field. The applied work maps to Assisting and Caring for Others and Documenting/Recording Information conducted with real clients, an in-person, judgment-laden activity task-exposure research does not classify as low-stakes. Assessing a client's functional needs and building an individualized treatment plan carries real error cost for a vulnerable population, keeping verification burden high, and the required field-application component adds embodied, real-time presence to the coursework. There is no general-studies lock, but the combination of client-facing judgment and field practice protects the course. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this hands-on clinical competence is intact.

By 2031, AI documentation tools will likely draft portions of treatment-plan paperwork and assessment templates, offloading some administrative writing, and diffusion of such tools into agency practice will be broader than it is today. But the core competence — assessing an individual client in person, exercising clinical judgment about treatment and program plans, and practicing community-integration skills with real people — remains high-verification, embodied clinical work where a misjudged assessment plan has direct consequences for a vulnerable client. That keeps a trained human necessary at the point of care. No institutional mandate protects the course structurally, but the dampening effect of high verification burden together with required in-field application holds the rating at Low across a catalog cycle; AI increasingly assists the paperwork, not the clinical judgment or the field practice itself.

A decade out, AI may handle more of the routine documentation and even suggest draft treatment-plan content, and the administrative shell of this work could automate further as capability and compute continue their fast growth trajectory. But the field-required core of the course — hands-on assessment, individualized planning judgment, and community-integration practice with real clients — remains embodied, high-stakes work whose failure modes are not obvious from a document alone, and the central case through 2036 keeps a knowledgeable, present human necessary for that judgment. The rating holds Low; the genuine uncertainty is how much of the surrounding paperwork automates around a still-human clinical assessment and field-practice core, not whether the applied competence itself remains instrumentally required for a student entering therapeutic recreation practice.
RECR 3530.d: This course will examine tools, techniques, and procedures utilized in the delivery of therapeutic recreation services. Assessment, individual treatment plans/program plans, documentation, and community integration skills are discussed. Application of content to practice in the field is required.

r: The seminar prepares recreation majors for an internship placement — goal setting, agency identification, evaluating supervisor qualifications, professional certification pathways, ethics, professional development planning, time management, and financial issues — entirely career-preparation and administrative content delivered through discussion and written planning documents, not the internship's actual field hours. This maps to Organizing, Planning, and Prioritizing Work, activities AI already assists competently, drafting goal statements, agency research summaries, and professional-development plans. The course carries no general-studies designation and, unlike the internship course itself, involves no supervised clock hours, so no F4 lock applies. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI meaningfully drafts career-planning and professional-development content, partially eroding the instrumental case for a seminar built around producing those documents, while near-term classroom adoption keeps the realized effect partial.

By 2031, AI career-coaching and planning tools will competently handle goal-setting, agency research, and professional-development documentation — the applied tasks this seminar's content addresses — and observed-usage data shows professional-writing and planning tasks as a substantial share of AI use. No general-studies mandate, licensure requirement, or supervised-hours structure protects this preparatory seminar, distinguishing it sharply from the internship course that follows it. The residual value — reflecting on one's own readiness and ethics before entering a professional placement — is real but is a narrower slice of the course's structured content than the planning-and-documentation work AI increasingly performs. The rating is High: the applied preparatory tasks are performed competently by AI with limited human input for most of the course's deliverables.

A decade out, AI career-preparation assistance is mature and likely embedded directly into how students plan internships, research agencies, and draft professional-development materials, and the applied tasks this seminar's content addresses are largely automatable given the sustained pace of capability and compute growth. With no institutional lock and no field-hour requirement of its own, little holds the rating back from High. The hedge is that ethical judgment and self-assessment before entering a vulnerable-population-facing placement may retain some irreducibly human component, and ten-year forecasts carry genuine uncertainty about how preparatory coursework is restructured under pervasive AI assistance. Contrasted with RECR 3980, the actual internship, this seminar's lack of embodied field hours is precisely why its trajectory diverges toward High rather than staying anchored at Low.
RECR 3870.d: The course prepares the recreation major for an internship placement in the recreation and parks field. Topics include goal setting, agency identification, supervisor qualifications, professional certification, ethics, professional development, time management, philosophy, and financial issues.

r: This is a supervised internship: students complete practical, hands-on experience in a professional recreation setting, with placements established and coordinated through the Classroom to Career Hub prior to enrollment, and faculty supervision throughout. The applied activity is embodied, in-person professional work — assisting and caring for participants, performing directly with the public, coordinating with agency staff — squarely in the least-automatable task-exposure categories. The binding constraint is course-specific and structural: the credit hours attach directly to verified, supervised placement hours in a real agency, a clock-hour requirement no AI system can satisfy on the student's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need for a student to physically complete supervised fieldwork is untouched; capability growth elsewhere in the field is simply not the operative variable for whether this course must be taken.

AI tools will increasingly appear inside recreation and park agencies by 2031 — scheduling, documentation, participant-engagement analytics — and interns will likely work alongside them as workplace diffusion continues to broaden. But the course's instrumental function is that a student personally accumulates supervised, verified professional hours in a real placement; that requirement is structural to the credit-hour design and does not loosen because agency work becomes more automated around the intern. Verification of readiness for the profession depends on faculty and site-supervisor observation of the student actually doing the work, keeping the embodied, real-time nature of the placement protective. The rating stays Low across this horizon: what AI changes is the content of the work being supervised, not whether supervised, hands-on placement hours remain required.

Even under a decade of substantial capability growth, a supervised internship's defining feature — the student physically present in a workplace, performing and being evaluated on real professional tasks under faculty and site oversight — is structurally resistant to substitution, because the requirement is the verified accumulation of hours, not merely the demonstration of knowledge. Recreation agencies will likely deploy considerably more AI-assisted tools by 2036, changing what interns do day to day, but that shift plausibly changes the content of supervised practice rather than removing the need for it. The rating holds Low, with the caveat that the balance of tasks an intern performs versus oversees may shift meaningfully, even as the clock-hour placement requirement itself persists in the central case.
RECR 3980.d: Supervised by a faculty member within the major department, internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to the major. Internship placements must be established prior to enrollment in this course in consultation with the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: The course examines contemporary issues in therapeutic recreation — standards of practice, ethical guidelines, credentials, professional philosophies, training and competency requirements, reimbursement, and research initiatives — a discussion-and-analysis seminar rather than a clinical-skills course. This maps to Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others, activities AI performs competently when synthesizing professional-issues literature and summarizing reimbursement or credentialing debates. The course sits near the end of the TR sequence with nothing else in the curriculum depending on it, and it carries no general-studies designation, so neither foundational scaffolding nor a transfer mandate protects it. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI already drafts competent issues analysis, partially eroding the rationale for a human-led discussion of this content, while near-term diffusion into how capstone-style seminars are taught keeps the realized effect only partial.

By 2031, AI will fluently synthesize and analyze professional issues in therapeutic recreation — credentialing debates, reimbursement policy, evolving standards of practice — and observed-usage data places explanatory and analytical writing among the more heavily used AI task categories. With no general-studies lock, no licensure-gated clinical hours attached to this specific course, and no downstream foundational role, little institutionally protects the rating from rising. The residual value — a practitioner's own synthesized judgment about where the field is heading — is real but narrower than the full survey-and-discussion content this seminar covers. The rating is High: the applied analytical work is performed competently by AI with limited human input across most of what the course teaches, leaving only professional interpretation to the student.

A decade out, AI is a capable synthesizer of professional-issues literature across credentialing, reimbursement policy, and evolving practice standards, and the applied analytical tasks this course's content serves are largely automatable, consistent with the sustained pace of capability and compute growth documented in the underlying trend evidence. Nothing embodied, licensure-gated, or foundational in this course's structure resists that trajectory, so the rating holds High, hedged by the possibility that professional judgment about applying evolving standards in one's own practice retains some irreducible human residue, and by the general uncertainty attached to any ten-year forecast. Relative to the clinically embodied TR courses in this sequence, this discussion-based issues seminar is comparatively exposed precisely because its content is analytical and its structure carries no protective institutional or foundational weight.
RECR 4030.d: This course focuses on contemporary issues impacting the profession in therapeutic recreation and includes topics such as standards of practice, ethical guidelines, credentials, philosophies, training and competency, reimbursement and research initiatives.

r: The course teaches intervention techniques applicable to leadership in therapeutic recreation, including individual and group facilitation techniques and development of a leisure-education program, with opportunities for involvement in clinical or community-based TR programs. This is advanced applied clinical leadership: leading facilitation sessions with real participants, adapting interventions in real time, and functioning inside an actual clinical or community program setting. These map to Assisting and Caring for Others and Guiding, Directing, and Motivating Subordinates, categories task-exposure research places among the least automatable because they require embodied, real-time, interpersonal presence with vulnerable populations. No general-studies designation applies, but embodiment alone protects this course. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop live facilitation competence with real clients is untouched — AI can describe intervention techniques, but it cannot lead the group or read a participant's response in the moment.

By 2031, AI may assist with drafting leisure-education program frameworks or generating intervention-technique reference material, offloading some preparatory planning as diffusion of such assistive tools broadens across the field. But the graded competence this advanced course builds — actually leading individual and group facilitation sessions inside clinical or community TR programs, adjusting technique to a real participant's needs in real time — remains embodied, high-verification clinical work; an error in facilitating a vulnerable client carries real consequence, keeping a trained human necessary at the point of delivery. No institutional mandate binds the course structurally, but the combination of low embodiment and real client-facing stakes holds the rating at Low across a catalog cycle. AI increasingly supports the planning layer, not the live facilitation itself.

Even a decade of substantial AI capability growth, consistent with the fast pace of underlying compute and capability trends, does not substitute for the specific competence this course develops — leading facilitation and intervention sessions with real people inside clinical or community therapeutic-recreation settings, where reading and responding to a participant in the moment is the point. The embodied, interpersonal core of advanced TR leadership sits within the least-automatable task-exposure category, and no licensure lock is needed for that protection to hold through 2036 in the central case. The rating stays Low; the honest uncertainty concerns how much programmatic planning and documentation around facilitation automates, not whether a student pursuing advanced TR practice still needs to personally develop the embodied leadership and facilitation skill this course builds.
RECR 4150.d: This course focuses on intervention techniques applicable to the leadership of therapeutic recreation. Individual and group facilitation techniques are discussed, including the development of a leisure-education program. Opportunities for involvement in clinical or community- based therapeutic recreation programs will be provided.

r: The course teaches students to understand funding sources for the health professions, locate funding agencies, and execute the grant-writing process, culminating in a full grant proposal written for a community agency — a purely desk-based research-and-writing task with no clinical, embodied, or field component. Grant and proposal writing map to Documenting/Recording Information and Communicating with Persons Outside Organization, activities close to the persuasive, researched-writing category task-exposure research and productivity studies both identify as highly automatable, with professional-writing RCTs showing large time savings and quality gains from AI assistance. The course carries no general-studies designation, no licensure mandate, and no foundational role for later coursework, so nothing institutionally protects it. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI already drafts competent grant narratives and locates funder information, but near-term classroom adoption of these tools remains partial.

By 2031, AI will competently draft full grant narratives, research funder priorities, and tailor proposal language to specific community agencies — essentially the entire applied task this course teaches — and professional-writing productivity research already shows AI assistance sharply cutting drafting time while improving perceived quality. With no general-studies lock, no clinical or licensure requirement, and no downstream course depending on it, nothing structurally caps the rating's rise. The residual competence — knowing an organization's real needs and verifying a funder-specific proposal's accuracy — is real but narrow relative to the drafting-and-research work this course centers on. The rating is High: the applied grant-writing work is performed competently by AI with limited human input for most of the deliverable, leaving mainly agency-relationship judgment to the human writer.

A decade out, AI grant-writing assistance is mature, fully capable of researching funders and producing polished, agency-tailored proposals, and the applied work this course's knowledge serves is almost entirely automatable — one of the more clear-cut high-exposure cases in the recreation curriculum because it combines a fully digital task with no institutional lock and no foundational role. The rating is High, hedged only by ten-year forecasting uncertainty and by the possibility that funders or agencies retain a preference for human-verified proposals in a landscape saturated with AI-generated applications. Among the courses in this batch, grant writing shows the clearest and least-protected exposure trajectory: nothing embodied, licensure-gated, or foundational holds back a task that sits squarely inside AI's demonstrated writing strengths.
RECR 4810.d: This course provides the student in the health professions with an understanding of funding sources, resources to locate funding agencies, and the grant writing process. Students will write a grant proposal for a community agency.

r: RECR 4890 places recreation, parks, and therapeutic recreation majors at agency sites for a mandated minimum of 480 clock hours over twelve weeks, rising to as many as 640 hours for students taking additional credit, performing program leadership, activity facilitation, participant supervision, session planning, and site documentation under a working professional supervisor. These tasks map to O*NET activities centered on assisting and caring for others, performing for or working directly with the public, coordinating group work, and monitoring participant safety in real time -- precisely the manual, physical, and interpersonal categories task-exposure research identifies as low-exposure relative to programming or writing work. The binding constraint is the course's own hard, course-specific mandate: a fixed clock-hour requirement completed only after core, concentration, and GPA prerequisites, structurally similar to a licensure-style practicum. At 24 months, AI tools may assist background planning but cannot log the hours or lead the embodied, supervised fieldwork itself, so the instrumental need is fully intact.

By 2031, AI scheduling and documentation tools will plausibly assist the agency side of an internship placement -- drafting program plans, tracking participant records, or summarizing incident reports -- but the graded work remains leading activities, supervising participants (including, in therapeutic recreation placements, clients with health or disability needs), and responding to real-time situations on site, none of which a model performs on the student's behalf. Diffusion data show AI adoption across firms is still uneven and lagging capability, so agency-level tool use is far from universal even where feasible. Verification burden stays meaningful: a supervisor observing a student's group-leadership and safety judgment cannot be replaced by an AI output check. The course's fixed clock-hour requirement, tied to senior-standing and concentration prerequisites, does not relax within a single catalog cycle. The instrumental case for completing this embodied placement remains essentially intact through 2031.

A decade out, under a wide central-case uncertainty band, AI will likely be embedded further into recreation-agency operations -- registration systems, adaptive-programming suggestions, participant-progress analytics -- and could meaningfully lighten the administrative shell around a placement. Capability growth on this horizon is fast by capability-trend estimates, but the embodied core this internship certifies -- a student personally leading activities, supervising participants' physical safety, and building professional judgment through 480 to 640 logged hours at a real agency -- is not a task an AI system performs in the student's place; it is a credentialing requirement about who the student demonstrably is. Task-exposure research continues to place manual, in-person, caregiving-adjacent work among the least automatable categories even as capability rises elsewhere. Barring a curricular change removing the clock-hour mandate itself, which is plausible only over a longer horizon, the instrumental need for this placement holds through 2036, with rising AI assistance around it rather than substitution for it.
RECR 4890.d: This course is designed to provide the recreation major with an intensive practical experience in the field of recreation, parks, or therapeutic recreation. Students must complete a minimum of 12 weeks with 480 clock hours at their agency for 10 credits. Each additional credit requires 40 more clock hours and 1 additional week at their agency for a maximum of 640 clock hours over 16 weeks.
